claim: In Arabidopsis, root hair and non-hair cell fates are determined by a MYB-bHLH-WD40 transcriptional complex.
source: In Arabidopsis, root hair and non-hair cell fates are determined by a MYB-bHLH-WD40 transcriptional complex and are regulated by many internal and environmental cues.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Arabidopsis root hair development.

claim: Root hair and non-hair cell fates are regulated by many internal and environmental cues.
source: In Arabidopsis, root hair and non-hair cell fates are determined by a MYB-bHLH-WD40 transcriptional complex and are regulated by many internal and environmental cues.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Brassinosteroids play important roles in regulating root hair specification.
source: Brassinosteroids play important roles in regulating root hair specification by unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact, though the mechanisms were previously unknown.

claim: Brassinosteroid signaling inhibits root hair formation through GSK3-like kinases or upstream components.
source: Here, we systematically examined root hair phenotypes in brassinosteroid-related mutants, and found that brassinosteroid signaling inhibits root hair formation through GSK3-like kinases or upstream components.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on systematic examination of mutants.

claim: With enhanced brassinosteroid signaling, GL2 is ectopically expressed in hair cells.
source: We found that with enhanced brassinosteroid signaling, GL2, a cell fate marker for non-hair cells, is ectopically expressed in hair cells, while its expression in non-hair cells is suppressed when brassinosteroid signaling is reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: GL2 expression in non-hair cells is suppressed when brassinosteroid signaling is reduced.
source: We found that with enhanced brassinosteroid signaling, GL2, a cell fate marker for non-hair cells, is ectopically expressed in hair cells, while its expression in non-hair cells is suppressed when brassinosteroid signaling is reduced.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: GL2 is a cell fate marker for non-hair cells.
source: We found that with enhanced brassinosteroid signaling, GL2, a cell fate marker for non-hair cells, is ectopically expressed in hair cells, while its expression in non-hair cells is suppressed when brassinosteroid signaling is reduced.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Brassinosteroid-regulated root epidermal cell patterning is dependent on the WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 transcriptional complex.
source: Genetic analysis demonstrated that brassinosteroid-regulated root epidermal cell patterning is dependent on the WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 transcriptional complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on genetic analysis.

claim: BIN2 interacted with EGL3.
source: One of the GSK3-like kinases, BIN2, interacted with and phosphorylated EGL3, and EGL3s mutated at phosphorylation sites were retained in hair cell nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: BIN2 phosphorylated EGL3.
source: One of the GSK3-like kinases, BIN2, interacted with and phosphorylated EGL3, and EGL3s mutated at phosphorylation sites were retained in hair cell nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: EGL3s mutated at phosphorylation sites were retained in hair cell nuclei.
source: One of the GSK3-like kinases, BIN2, interacted with and phosphorylated EGL3, and EGL3s mutated at phosphorylation sites were retained in hair cell nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: BIN2 phosphorylated TTG1 to inhibit the activity of the WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 complex.
source: BIN2 phosphorylated TTG1 to inhibit the activity of the WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Hair cells (trichoblasts) are specified early from root epidermal cells that lie over clefts between two underlying cortical cells.
source: Hair (H) cells, or trichoblasts, are specified early from root epidermal cells that lie over clefts between two underlying cortical cells, whereas the root epidermal cells that lie over a single cortical cell develop as non-hair (N) cells, or atrichoblasts (Ishida et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Root epidermal cells that lie over a single cortical cell develop as non-hair cells (atrichoblasts).
source: Hair (H) cells, or trichoblasts, are specified early from root epidermal cells that lie over clefts between two underlying cortical cells, whereas the root epidermal cells that lie over a single cortical cell develop as non-hair (N) cells, or atrichoblasts (Ishida et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Hair cell and non-hair cell files are patterned alternately in rows within the Arabidopsis root epidermis.
source: Hair cell and non-hair cell files are patterned alternately in rows within the Arabidopsis root epidermis, with columns of hair cells interspersed with columns of non-hair cells (Schiefelbein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Root epidermal cells in the H position have a greater rate of cell division than those in the N position.
source: Prior to root hair outgrowth, root epidermal cells in the H position can be distinguished from those in the N position by many visible cellular features, including a greater rate of cell division (Berger et al., 1998), reduced cell length and vacuolation (Dolan et al., 1994; Galway et al., 1994), and enhanced cytoplasmic density (Dolan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Root epidermal cells in the H position have reduced cell length and vacuolation compared to those in the N position.
source: Prior to root hair outgrowth, root epidermal cells in the H position can be distinguished from those in the N position by many visible cellular features, including a greater rate of cell division (Berger et al., 1998), reduced cell length and vacuolation (Dolan et al., 1994; Galway et al., 1994), and enhanced cytoplasmic density (Dolan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Root epidermal cells in the H position have enhanced cytoplasmic density compared to those in the N position.
source: Prior to root hair outgrowth, root epidermal cells in the H position can be distinguished from those in the N position by many visible cellular features, including a greater rate of cell division (Berger et al., 1998), reduced cell length and vacuolation (Dolan et al., 1994; Galway et al., 1994), and enhanced cytoplasmic density (Dolan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Positional signals and SCRAMBLED (SCM) function through a MYB-bHLH-WD40 repeat transcriptional complex to determine root epidermal cell fate.
source: It is proposed that positional signals and a putative receptor-like kinase SCRAMBLED (SCM) (Kwak et al., 2005) function through a MYB-bHLH-WD40 repeat transcriptional complex to determine root epidermal cell fate (Schiefelbein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed model with citations.

claim: In N cells, WEREWOLF (WER) forms a complex with GL3/EGL3 and TTG1 to promote expression of GLABRA2 (GL2) and CAPRICE (CPC).
source: Based on this model, in N cells, WEREWOLF (WER) (Lee and Schiefelbein, 1999), a R2R3 MYB-domain transcription factor, forms a complex with basic helix-loop-helix transcription factors, GLABRA3 (GL3)/ENHANCER OF GLABRA3 (EGL3) (Bernhardt et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2003), and a WD40 repeat protein, TRANSPARENT TESTA GLABRA1 (TTG1) (Galway et al., 1994), to promote expression of GLABRA2 (GL2) and CAPRICE (CPC) (Ryu et al., 2005; Song et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as part of an established model with citations.

claim: GL2 negatively regulates H cell fate and positively regulates N cell fate.
source: GL2, a homeodomain/leucine zipper transcription factor, negatively regulates H cell fate and positively regulates N cell fate (Masucci et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: CPC moves from N cells to H cells.
source: CPC (Wada et al., 1997), a MYB-type transcription factor, moves from N cells to H cells (Kurata et al., 2005a) to compete with WER for binding to GL3/EGL3 to form a CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 complex, which is unable to induce GL2 expression (Song et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: CPC competes with WER for binding to GL3/EGL3 to form a CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 complex.
source: CPC (Wada et al., 1997), a MYB-type transcription factor, moves from N cells to H cells (Kurata et al., 2005a) to compete with WER for binding to GL3/EGL3 to form a CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 complex, which is unable to induce GL2 expression (Song et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 complex is unable to induce GL2 expression.
source: CPC (Wada et al., 1997), a MYB-type transcription factor, moves from N cells to H cells (Kurata et al., 2005a) to compete with WER for binding to GL3/EGL3 to form a CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 complex, which is unable to induce GL2 expression (Song et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: GL3 is a mobile protein.
source: In addition to CPC, the bHLH transcription factor GL3 is also a mobile protein (Bernhardt et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: GL3 and EGL3 are both expressed in H cells.
source: GL3 and its homologue EGL3 are both expressed in H cells, but GL3 protein is only localized in the N cell nucleus, indicating that GL3 protein moves into the adjoining N cell nucleus to determine N cell fate (Bernhardt et al., 2003, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: GL3 protein is only localized in the N cell nucleus.
source: GL3 and its homologue EGL3 are both expressed in H cells, but GL3 protein is only localized in the N cell nucleus, indicating that GL3 protein moves into the adjoining N cell nucleus to determine N cell fate (Bernhardt et al., 2003, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: GL3 protein moves into the adjoining N cell nucleus to determine N cell fate.
source: GL3 and its homologue EGL3 are both expressed in H cells, but GL3 protein is only localized in the N cell nucleus, indicating that GL3 protein moves into the adjoining N cell nucleus to determine N cell fate (Bernhardt et al., 2003, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from established knowledge with citations.

claim: Abscisic acid (ABA) plays a role in the early stage of root epidermal cell specification.
source: For instance, abscisic acid (ABA) plays a role in the early stage of root epidermal cell specification (Van Hengel et al., 2004) and in inhibiting root hair tip growth in Arabidopsis (Schnall and Quatrano, 1992), while both ethylene and auxin may act downstream of TTG1 and GL2 to promote root hair formation and elongation (Masucci and Schiefelbein, 1994, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: ABA inhibits root hair tip growth in Arabidopsis.

claim: Jasmonic acids (JAs) promote root hair formation through their interaction with ethylene.
source: Moreover, jasmonic acids (JAs) promote root hair formation through their interaction with ethylene (Zhu et al., 2006).

claim: Brassinosteroids (BRs) play essential roles in regulating shoot, root, and reproductive development.
source: The plant steroid hormones, brassinosteroids (BRs), play essential roles in regulating many developmental processes, including shoot, root, and reproductive development (Savaldi-Goldstein et al., 2007; Ye et al., 2010; Hacham et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: BRs are perceived by the receptor kinase BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1 (BRI1).
source: BRs are perceived by the receptor kinase BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 1 (BRI1) (Li and Chory, 1997; Hothorn et al., 2011; She et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: BR-activated BRI1 phosphorylates BRI1 KINASE INHIBITOR 1 (BKI1) to release its inhibition.
source: The BR-activated BRI1 phosphorylates BRI1 KINASE INHIBITOR 1 (BKI1) to release its inhibition (Wang and Chory, 2006), and then BKI1 acts as a positive regulator by binding to a subset of 14-3-3 proteins (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: BKI1 acts as a positive regulator by binding to a subset of 14-3-3 proteins.

source: Another BRI1 substrate, BR-SIGNALING KINASE (BSK), transduces the BR signaling through bri1 SUPPRESSORS 1 (BSU1) to inactivate a GSK3-like kinase BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 2 (BIN2), which leads to accumulation of the dephosphorylated form of transcriptional factors BRI1 EMS SUPPRESSOR 1 (BES1)/BRASSINAZOLE RESISTANT 1 (BZR1) in the nucleus to regulate gene expression (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Inactivation of BIN2 leads to accumulation of the dephosphorylated form of BES1/BZR1 in the nucleus to regulate gene expression.
source: Another BRI1 substrate, BR-SIGNALING KINASE (BSK), transduces the BR signaling through bri1 SUPPRESSORS 1 (BSU1) to inactivate a GSK3-like kinase BRASSINOSTEROID INSENSITIVE 2 (BIN2), which leads to accumulation of the dephosphorylated form of transcriptional factors BRI1 EMS SUPPRESSOR 1 (BES1)/BRASSINAZOLE RESISTANT 1 (BZR1) in the nucleus to regulate gene expression (Yang et al., 2011).

source: In contrast, GL2 was ectopically expressed in about 13.5% of H cells in BRI1-OX plants (Figure 2J–L) and in about 19.6% in bin2-3 bil1 bil2 (Figure 2M–O), as compared with only 3.2% in the wild type (Figure 2A–C), indicating that lack of GL2 expression in N cells may correspond to the ectopic root hairs observed in bri1-116 and det2-1, and that the ectopically expressed GL2 in H cells partially inhibits H cell fate in BRI1-OX and bin2-3 bil1 bil2 plants.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of ectopic GL2 expression in H cells.

claim: BR signaling has an important role in suppressing H cell fate and promoting N cell fate in both the N and the H positions.
source: Taken together, the above results suggested that BR signaling has an important role in suppressing H cell fate and promoting N cell fate in both the N and the H positions, and BR signaling regulates root epidermal cell fate by controlling GL2 expression through GSK3-like kinases, or their upstream components, but not through downstream transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: BR signaling regulates root epidermal cell fate by controlling GL2 expression through GSK3-like kinases, or their upstream components, but not through downstream transcription factors.
source: Taken together, the above results suggested that BR signaling has an important role in suppressing H cell fate and promoting N cell fate in both the N and the H positions, and BR signaling regulates root epidermal cell fate by controlling GL2 expression through GSK3-like kinases, or their upstream components, but not through downstream transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: GL2 expression is directly regulated by the WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 but not the CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 transcriptional complex.
source: It was known that GL2 expression is directly regulated by the WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 but not the CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 transcriptional complex (Schiefelbein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: cpc-1 is a mutant with fewer root hairs than its counterpart.
source: To explore whether the BR-regulated GL2 expression and root epidermal cell fate determination are dependent on these complexes, we first created a set of double mutants of cpc-1, a mutant with fewer root hairs than its counterpart (Figure 3A,B), with bri1-116 or cpd (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a primary observation from the study with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Both double mutants bri1-116 cpc-1 and cpd cpc-1 produced few root hairs, similar to cpc-1.
source: Similar to cpc-1, both double mutants bri1-116 cpc-1 (Figure 3E) and cpd cpc-1 (Figure 3F) produced few root hairs.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the study with reference to Figure 3.

claim: wer-1 is a mutant with more root hairs than Col-0.
source: We also generated double or multiple mutants of wer-1, a mutant with more root hairs than Col-0 (Figure 3G,H), with BRI1-OX or bin2-3 bil1 bil2 (Figure 3I,J), and found that both BRI1-OX wer-1 and bin2-3 bil1 bil2 wer-1 (Figure 3K,L) were similar to wer-1, with many ectopic root hairs formed at the N cell position.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the study with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Both BRI1-OX wer-1 and bin2-3 bil1 bil2 wer-1 were similar to wer-1, with many ectopic root hairs formed at the N cell position.
source: We also generated double or multiple mutants of wer-1, a mutant with more root hairs than Col-0 (Figure 3G,H), with BRI1-OX or bin2-3 bil1 bil2 (Figure 3I,J), and found that both BRI1-OX wer-1 and bin2-3 bil1 bil2 wer-1 (Figure 3K,L) were similar to wer-1, with many ectopic root hairs formed at the N cell position.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the study with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 and CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 transcriptional complexes act downstream of BR early signaling.
source: These genetic analyses indicated that the WER-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 and CPC-GL3/EGL3-TTG1 transcriptional complexes act downstream of BR early signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic analysis of double mutants.

claim: BIN2 can interact with EGL3 in yeast.
source: We then conducted yeast two-hybrid assays to test whether any components in the WER-EGL3/GL3-TTG1 or CPC-EGL3/GL3-TTG1 complex interact with BIN2, a well-studied GSK3-like kinase, and found that BIN2 can interact with EGL3 (Figure 4A) but not with CPC in yeast (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from yeast two-hybrid assays with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: BIN2 does not interact with CPC in yeast.
source: We then conducted yeast two-hybrid assays to test whether any components in the WER-EGL3/GL3-TTG1 or CPC-EGL3/GL3-TTG1 complex interact with BIN2, a well-studied GSK3-like kinase, and found that BIN2 can interact with EGL3 (Figure 4A) but not with CPC in yeast (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from yeast two-hybrid assays with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: BIN2 can interact with WER, EGL3, and TTG1 in GST pull-down and BiFC assays.
source: However, due to strong auto-activation of WER and TTG1 fused with GAL4-DNA binding domain (DB) in yeast two-hybrid assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we conducted GST pull-down and BiFC (biomolecular fluorescence complementation) assays to test their interactions, and found that BIN2 can interact with WER, EGL3, and TTG1 (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from GST pull-down and BiFC assays with reference to Figure 4B,C.

claim: BIN2 did not phosphorylate WER and CPC.
source: We found that BIN2 did not phosphorylate WER and CPC, but was able to phosphorylate EGL3 and TTG1 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays with reference to Figure 5.

claim: BIN2 was able to phosphorylate EGL3 and TTG1.
source: We found that BIN2 did not phosphorylate WER and CPC, but was able to phosphorylate EGL3 and TTG1 (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro kinase assays with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Four potential phosphorylation sites (T209, T213, T399, and T403) of EGL3 by BIN2 were identified using mass spectrometry.
source: To investigate the biological relevance of EGL3 phosphorylation by a GSK3-like kinase BIN2, we used mass spectrometry and identified four potential phosphorylation sites (T209, T213, T399, and T403) of EGL3 by BIN2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which are located in two regions that contain typical recognition sites of GSK3 kinases (Cohen and Frame, 2001).
evidence: This is a primary finding from mass spectrometry analysis with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phosphorylation sites T209, T213, T399, and T403 are located in two regions that contain typical recognition sites of GSK3 kinases.
source: To investigate the biological relevance of EGL3 phosphorylation by a GSK3-like kinase BIN2, we used mass spectrometry and identified four potential phosphorylation sites (T209, T213, T399, and T403) of EGL3 by BIN2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which are located in two regions that contain typical recognition sites of GSK3 kinases (Cohen and Frame, 2001).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to established knowledge about GSK3 kinase recognition sites.

claim: Phosphorylation levels of EGL3T399A and EGL3T209A/T213A by BIN2 were significantly reduced.
source: In vitro phosphorylation assays showed that phosphorylation levels of EGL3T399A and EGL3T209A/T213A by BIN2 were significantly reduced (Figure 6A), indicating that T399 and T209/T213 are the main phosphorylated residues.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro phosphorylation assays with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: T399 and T209/T213 are the main phosphorylated residues of EGL3 by BIN2.
source: In vitro phosphorylation assays showed that phosphorylation levels of EGL3T399A and EGL3T209A/T213A by BIN2 were significantly reduced (Figure 6A), indicating that T399 and T209/T213 are the main phosphorylated residues.
evidence: This is an inference from the reduced phosphorylation of mutated forms.

claim: The EGL3-GFP signal in N cells was apparently higher than that in H cells.
source: We found that the EGL3-GFP signal in N cells was apparently higher than that in H cells, and that it was mainly localized to cytosol in H cells, but to both cytosol and nucleus in N cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary observation from transgenic plants with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: EGL3-GFP was mainly localized to cytosol in H cells, but to both cytosol and nucleus in N cells.
source: We found that the EGL3-GFP signal in N cells was apparently higher than that in H cells, and that it was mainly localized to cytosol in H cells, but to both cytosol and nucleus in N cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary observation from transgenic plants with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: EGL3 is a mobile protein that moves from H cells to N cells.
source: As EGL3 mRNA is only expressed in H cells (Bernhardt et al., 2005), this result indicated that, like its homologue GL3, EGL3 is also a mobile protein that moves from H cells to N cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that EGL3 protein is found in N cells despite mRNA expression only in H cells.

claim: EGL3T399A-GFP and EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP were solely localized to the nuclei of H cells.
source: However, the EGL3T399A-GFP and EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP were solely localized to the nuclei of H cells (Figure 6C,D), indicating that EGL3 phosphorylation is required not only for its cytoplasmic accumulation, but also for its movement from H cells to N cells.
evidence: This is a primary observation from transgenic plants with reference to Figure 6C,D.

claim: EGL3 phosphorylation is required for its cytoplasmic accumulation and for its movement from H cells to N cells.
source: However, the EGL3T399A-GFP and EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP were solely localized to the nuclei of H cells (Figure 6C,D), indicating that EGL3 phosphorylation is required not only for its cytoplasmic accumulation, but also for its movement from H cells to N cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that non-phosphorylatable mutants are retained in H cell nuclei.

claim: The root hair patterning of EGL3-GFP transgenic plants was not altered.
source: In addition, we found that the root hair patterning of EGL3-GFP transgenic plants was not altered (Figure 6E; Table 1), indicating that correctly localized EGL3, mainly in N cell nuclei to promote N cell fate and less in H cell nuclei not to promote N cell fate, has no influence on root epidermal fate.
evidence: This is a primary observation from transgenic plants with reference to Figure 6E and Table 1.

claim: Root epidermal patterning in the EGL3T399A-GFP transgenic plants was normal.
source: Moreover, although root epidermal patterning in the EGL3T399A-GFP transgenic plants was normal (Figure 6F; Table 1), the number of root hairs in EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP plants was significantly reduced, likely due to a misspecification of non-hair cells in the H position (Figure 6G; Table 1), suggesting that the nucleus-localized EGL3 in H cells may determine N cell fate specification.
evidence: This is a primary observation from transgenic plants with reference to Figure 6F and Table 1.

claim: The number of root hairs in EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP plants was significantly reduced, likely due to a misspecification of non-hair cells in the H position.
source: Moreover, although root epidermal patterning in the EGL3T399A-GFP transgenic plants was normal (Figure 6F; Table 1), the number of root hairs in EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP plants was significantly reduced, likely due to a misspecification of non-hair cells in the H position (Figure 6G; Table 1), suggesting that the nucleus-localized EGL3 in H cells may determine N cell fate specification.
evidence: This is a primary observation from transgenic plants with reference to Figure 6G and Table 1.

claim: The nucleus-localized EGL3 in H cells may determine N cell fate specification.
source: Moreover, although root epidermal patterning in the EGL3T399A-GFP transgenic plants was normal (Figure 6F; Table 1), the number of root hairs in EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP plants was significantly reduced, likely due to a misspecification of non-hair cells in the H position (Figure 6G; Table 1), suggesting that the nucleus-localized EGL3 in H cells may determine N cell fate specification.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that nucleus-localized EGL3 mutants reduce root hair number.

claim: BIN2 phosphorylation on T399, T209, and/or T213 of EGL3 in H cells promotes EGL3 cytoplasmic localization, which likely helps its movement from H to N cells to regulate root epidermal cell fate.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that BIN2 phosphorylation on T399, T209, and/or T213 of EGL3 in H cells promotes EGL3 cytoplasmic localization, which likely helps its movement from H to N cells to regulate root epidermal cell fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: TTG1 is required for a normal expression level of GL2.
source: TTG1 is required for a normal expression level of GL2 (Di Cristina et al., 1996) but not for its expression pattern (Hung et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: TTG1 is not required for GL2 expression pattern.
source: TTG1 is required for a normal expression level of GL2 (Di Cristina et al., 1996) but not for its expression pattern (Hung et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: TTG1 was preferentially localized in the cytoplasm and slightly in the nucleus of both N and H cells.
source: Transgenic TTG1-GFP plants driven by its own promoter indicated that TTG1 was preferentially localized in the cytoplasm and slightly in the nucleus of both N and H cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which was consistent with the subcellular localization of its petunia homologue AN11 (De Vetten et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a primary observation from transgenic plants with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The subcellular localization of TTG1 is consistent with the subcellular localization of its petunia homologue AN11.
source: Transgenic TTG1-GFP plants driven by its own promoter indicated that TTG1 was preferentially localized in the cytoplasm and slightly in the nucleus of both N and H cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which was consistent with the subcellular localization of its petunia homologue AN11 (De Vetten et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to established knowledge.

claim: Transient expression of WER alone was able to slightly induce PGL2::LUC gene expression.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, transient expression of WER alone was able to slightly induce PGL2::LUC gene expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transient transcription assays with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Transient expression of EGL3 alone was unable to induce reporter gene expression.
source: In contrast, transient expression of EGL3 alone was unable to induce reporter gene expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transient transcription assays.

claim: Co-expression of WER and EGL3 can dramatically promote LUC expression.
source: Co-expression of WER and EGL3 can dramatically promote LUC expression, which is consistent with a previous study (Song et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding from transient transcription assays with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Additional bin2-1 did not alter the effect of WER, EGL3, or both WER and EGL3 on PGL2::LUC expression.
source: Additional bin2-1 did not alter the effect of WER, EGL3, or both WER and EGL3 on PGL2::LUC expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transient transcription assays.

claim: When WER, EGL3, and TTG1 were used together, the expression of PGL2::LUC was further enhanced.
source: When WER, EGL3, and TTG1 were used together, the expression of PGL2::LUC was further enhanced, indicating that TTG1 can promote the activity of the WER-EGL3 complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transient transcription assays.

claim: TTG1 can promote the activity of the WER-EGL3 complex.
source: When WER, EGL3, and TTG1 were used together, the expression of PGL2::LUC was further enhanced, indicating that TTG1 can promote the activity of the WER-EGL3 complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that TTG1 enhances reporter expression.

claim: Additional bin2-1 significantly inhibited reporter gene expression regulated by the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex.
source: Interestingly, additional bin2-1 significantly inhibited reporter gene expression regulated by the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex (Figure 7B), indicating that TTG1 is mediating the negative effect of BIN2 on this transcriptional complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from transient transcription assays with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: TTG1 is mediating the negative effect of BIN2 on the WER-EGL3-TTG1 transcriptional complex.
source: Interestingly, additional bin2-1 significantly inhibited reporter gene expression regulated by the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex (Figure 7B), indicating that TTG1 is mediating the negative effect of BIN2 on this transcriptional complex.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that BIN2 only inhibits the complex when TTG1 is present.

claim: BR signaling depends on GSK3-like kinases and the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex to modulate root epidermal patterning.
source: We provide several lines of evidence to strongly support an important role for BR signaling in directly regulating root hair cell fate. First, root hair patterning in the BR-biosynthetic and responsive mutants or in the wild type grown on eBL, bikinin, or BRZ, was dramatically altered, demonstrating that GSK3 kinases and/or their upstream components are mediating this regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: BR early signaling promotes N cell fate in the whole root epidermis.
source: Second, the expression pattern of the non-hair cell fate marker PGL2::GUS indicates that BR early signaling promotes N cell fate in the whole root epidermis, which is a reasonable explanation for the abnormal root hair patterning in the BR-related mutants: when BR signaling is enhanced, fewer root hairs are formed in the H position; when BR signaling is inhibited, more ectopic root hairs are produced in the N position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PGL2::GUS expression pattern analysis.

claim: Major components of the WER-EGL3-TTG1 or CPC-EGL3-TTG1 complex act downstream of BR signaling-mediated root epidermis patterning.
source: Third, genetic analysis revealed that major components of the WER-EGL3-TTG1 or CPC-EGL3-TTG1 complex act downstream of BR signaling-mediated root epidermis patterning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic analysis.

claim: GSK3-like kinases directly regulate EGL3 movement and the transcription activity of the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex to mediate root hair development.
source: Finally, BIN2 phosphorylation on EGL3 and TTG1 suggested that GSK3-like kinases directly regulate EGL3 movement and the transcription activity of the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex to mediate root hair development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phosphorylation studies.

claim: Cytoplasmic localization of mobile proteins may be required for their intercellular movement.
source: Non-cell autonomous movement of some transcriptional factors is an important mechanism to regulate some developmental processes (Kurata et al., 2005b), and cytoplasmic localization of these mobile proteins may be required for their intercellular movement.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: A mutation in the potential nuclear localization signal (NLS) of KNOTTED 1 abolished its intercellular movement in maize shoot apical meristem.
source: For example, in maize shoot apical meristem, a mutation in its potential nuclear localization signal (NLS) of KNOTTED 1 abolished its intercellular movement (Vollbrecht et al., 1991; Lucas et al., 1995), and cytoplasmic localization of LEAFY (Schultz and Haughn, 1991), a transcriptional factor in floral identity, is also strongly correlated with its adjacent cell movement (Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Cytoplasmic localization of LEAFY is strongly correlated with its adjacent cell movement.
source: For example, in maize shoot apical meristem, a mutation in its potential nuclear localization signal (NLS) of KNOTTED 1 abolished its intercellular movement (Vollbrecht et al., 1991; Lucas et al., 1995), and cytoplasmic localization of LEAFY (Schultz and Haughn, 1991), a transcriptional factor in floral identity, is also strongly correlated with its adjacent cell movement (Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The movement of SHORT-ROOT was abolished when it was fused to a NLS, leading to its diminished cytoplasmic localization.
source: Moreover, the movement of SHORT-ROOT, another mobile transcriptional factor in root radical patterning (Helariutta et al., 2000), was abolished when it was fused to a NLS, leading to its diminished cytoplasmic localization (Gallagher et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: T399 is located in a predicted non-canonical NLS of EGL3.
source: Although we do not know how T209/T213 phosphorylation regulated EGL3 subcellular localization, the T399 phosphorylation likely affected a NLS, because T399 is located in a predicted non-canonical NLS (Figure 6—source data 1), which is found in many other plant bHLHs (Galstyan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—source data 1 and a citation.

claim: Non-canonical NLS is found in many other plant bHLHs.
source: Although we do not know how T209/T213 phosphorylation regulated EGL3 subcellular localization, the T399 phosphorylation likely affected a NLS, because T399 is located in a predicted non-canonical NLS (Figure 6—source data 1), which is found in many other plant bHLHs (Galstyan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The nucleus-localized EGL3T399A in H cells is unable to induce GL2 expression, likely because T399 is close to the bHLH domain which may have affected its interaction with TTG1 and MYB.
source: Although the EGL3T399A-GFP plants showed normal root hair patterning, this can be explained by the close proximity of T399 to its bHLH domain, which may have affected its interaction with TTG1 and MYB (Zhang et al., 2003), leading to the nucleus-localized EGL3T399A in H cells unable to induce GL2 expression.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the normal root hair patterning in EGL3T399A-GFP plants.

claim: EGL3T209A/T213A may still interact with TTG1 and have DNA-binding activity because T209/T213 is located in the N-terminal region far away from the bHLH domain.
source: However, EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP may still interact with TTG1 and have DNA-binding activity, because T209/T213 was located in the N-terminal region far away from the bHLH domain (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which led to GL2 expression in H cells and EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP plants growing fewer root hairs (Figure 6G; Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference to explain the reduced root hair phenotype in EGL3T209A/T213A-GFP plants.

claim: TTG1 interacts with EGL3.
source: Furthermore, it was reported that TTG1 interacts with EGL3 (Zhang et al., 2003), and TTG1 is necessary for the full functioning of other bHLH partners, such as GL3 and TRANSPARENT TESTA8 (Baudry et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: TTG1 is necessary for the full functioning of other bHLH partners, such as GL3 and TRANSPARENT TESTA8.
source: Furthermore, it was reported that TTG1 interacts with EGL3 (Zhang et al., 2003), and TTG1 is necessary for the full functioning of other bHLH partners, such as GL3 and TRANSPARENT TESTA8 (Baudry et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: TTG1 phosphorylation by GSK3-like kinases may affect its regulation of EGL3 and the activity of the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex.
source: Therefore, it is very likely that TTG1 phosphorylation by GSK3-like kinases may affect its regulation of EGL3 and the activity of the WER-EGL3-TTG1 complex.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: The N cell is a default cell type in root epidermis.
source: Our data also support the suggestion that the N cell is a default cell type in root epidermis, and that H cell fate is produced due to inhibition of N cell fate by internal or external cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: H cell fate is produced due to inhibition of N cell fate by internal or external cues.
source: Our data also support the suggestion that the N cell is a default cell type in root epidermis, and that H cell fate is produced due to inhibition of N cell fate by internal or external cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: WER is expressed in both N and H cells in the early root meristem.
source: First, we observed that WER, a positive regulator for GL2 expression, is expressed in both N and H cells in the early root meristem (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), which is also supported by a previous report that WER exhibits uniform promoter activity in both N and H cells proximal to the initial cells (Savage et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a primary observation from the study with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: Over-expression of GL3 and EGL3 promoted non-hair cell fate.
source: Moreover, over-expression of GL3 and EGL3 promoted non-hair cell fate (Bernhardt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: TTG1 is localized in both N and H cells.
source: Third, TTG1 is localized in both N and H cells, and TTG1 and EGL3 may synergistically promote WER-EGL3 transcriptional activity and enhance N cell fate.
evidence: This is stated based on the study's findings.

claim: TTG1 and EGL3 may synergistically promote WER-EGL3 transcriptional activity and enhance N cell fate.
source: Third, TTG1 is localized in both N and H cells, and TTG1 and EGL3 may synergistically promote WER-EGL3 transcriptional activity and enhance N cell fate.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: BR signaling promotes WER expression.
source: Apparently, BR signaling can promote N cell fate in several ways. Besides the inhibition of BR signaling on EGL3 cell–cell movement and the promotion of TTG1 activity, BR signaling also promotes WER expression as WER up-regulation in bin2-3 bil1 bil2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with the positive role of BRs in WER expression (Kuppusamy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on the study's findings with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: WER is up-regulated in bin2-3 bil1 bil2.
source: Apparently, BR signaling can promote N cell fate in several ways. Besides the inhibition of BR signaling on EGL3 cell–cell movement and the promotion of TTG1 activity, BR signaling also promotes WER expression as WER up-regulation in bin2-3 bil1 bil2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with the positive role of BRs in WER expression (Kuppusamy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 1.
